title: FSSAI Penalises Fortune Oil Maker AWL After Sunflower Oil Fails Vitamin D Test
excerpt: India's food safety regulator has taken action against AWL Agri Business, formerly Adani Wilmar, after a Fortune sunflower oil sample did not meet mandatory Vitamin D fortification standards, part of an intensifying crackdown on food labelling and quality.
body:
• FSSAI has penalised AWL Agri Business (formerly Adani Wilmar), the maker of Fortune brand cooking oils, after a sunflower oil sample failed to meet prescribed Vitamin D fortification standards.
  • The action is part of a broader FSSAI crackdown that has targeted Dabur, Diageo and over a dozen food companies in recent weeks for misleading claims, labelling violations and quality failures.
  • Fortune is India's largest edible oil brand; AWL operates 24 plants across 11 states and reported revenue of 75,148 crore rupees in FY2026.
  • Consumer advocates say FSSAI's maximum penalty of 10 lakh rupees under the 2006 Food Safety Act is inadequate for companies of AWL's scale.

Fortification Standards at Issue

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has penalised AWL Agri Business, the company behind India's best-selling Fortune brand of cooking oils, after a sample of its refined sunflower oil failed to meet the mandatory Vitamin D fortification standard during routine testing.

Under FSSAI's Food Safety and Standards (Fortification of Foods) Regulations, edible oils sold in India must be fortified with Vitamins A and D to address widespread micronutrient deficiencies. The regulations specify minimum levels of these vitamins that must be present at the point of sale. The Fortune sunflower oil sample in question did not meet the prescribed Vitamin D threshold, triggering regulatory action.

AWL Agri Business — formerly Adani Wilmar until the Adani Group sold its stake to Singapore's Wilmar International in 2025 — is India's largest edible oil processor. The company operates 24 plants across 11 states, exports to more than 50 countries, and reported revenue of 75,148 crore rupees ($7.8 billion) in the last fiscal year. Fortune is its flagship brand, sold through roughly 900,000 retail outlets nationwide.

Part of a Wider Crackdown

The action against AWL comes amid a sweeping FSSAI enforcement drive that has made the food safety regulator one of India's most active regulatory bodies in recent months. In the first week of August alone, FSSAI barred Dabur India from selling products carrying unverified "100% Natural" and "100% Pure" claims, and prohibited the sale of certain Diageo and Inbrew liquor products found to contain artificial flavouring substances.

Earlier this year, the regulator issued notices to 14 food business operators — including makers of cooking oils, beverages, packaged foods and health supplements — for misleading health claims and labelling violations. FSSAI also sent notices to Heritage Foods, Dia Foods and Cipzer Nutraceuticals over claims such as "Fresh Paneer," "All Natural" and "FSSAI approved" that the regulator deemed deceptive.

"Food labelling is not merely a marketing tool but a critical source of information that consumers rely on while making purchasing decisions."

— FSSAI statement

Fortification: Why It Matters for Indian Kitchens

India's oil fortification mandate addresses a significant public health challenge. According to the National Family Health Survey, over 70 per cent of Indians have insufficient Vitamin D levels, contributing to bone disorders, weakened immunity and developmental issues in children. Fortifying cooking oil — a staple consumed across income levels — has been one of the government's primary strategies to close the micronutrient gap at population scale.

When a major brand like Fortune falls short of fortification standards, the impact is amplified by its sheer market reach. AWL's oils are used in millions of Indian households daily, and consumers who purchase fortified products expect to receive the nutritional benefits advertised on the label.

Enforcement Gap Remains

Consumer advocates have pointed to a structural limitation in India's food safety framework. Under the Food Safety and Standards Act of 2006, FSSAI can impose a maximum financial penalty of 10 lakh rupees — a figure that has remained unchanged for nearly two decades. For a company generating annual revenue in the tens of thousands of crores, such penalties represent a negligible fraction of turnover.

A recent investigation found that of 163 products flagged by FSSAI for misleading claims since 2022, nearly 120 remained in circulation with the same packaging and claims intact. The finding has intensified calls for legislative reform to give the regulator stronger enforcement tools, including higher penalties, mandatory product recalls and the authority to suspend manufacturing licences for repeat offenders.

For Consumers: Read Beyond the Label

The FSSAI has advised consumers to examine nutrition information panels and look for the '+F' logo that indicates fortified products, rather than relying on front-of-pack marketing claims. Regulators have also urged consumers to report quality concerns through the Food Safety Connect app or the toll-free helpline at 1800-112-100.

AWL Agri Business has previously stated that it places great importance on nutritional value that consumers seek in their grocery choices. The company's response to the latest penalty and any corrective measures it plans to implement will be closely watched by regulators, competitors and the millions of Indian households that stock Fortune oil in their kitchens.
nri_angle: Fortune is widely available in Indian grocery stores across the US, UK and Canada; diaspora consumers buying imported Fortune oil should check fortification labels.
